title: Browser Automation Basics (Selenium and Playwright)
summary: Sometimes an app has no API and no integration - you can only use it through its website - and that is exactly when browser automation saves the day by controlling a real browser the way a human would. Tools like Selenium and Playwright launch Chrome
content:
# Browser Automation Basics (Selenium and Playwright) ##### The portal with no API A logistics client had one process that resisted every attempt at automation. Every morning, someone logged into a state transport department portal, entered a permit number, waited for a page to load, and copied a status value into a spreadsheet. Forty permits, forty-five minutes, every single day. There was no API. There was no export. There was no integration in any iPaaS. There was no vendor to email. The portal was built in 2011 and the department had no interest in changing it. This is the exact situation **browser automation** exists for. You write a script that drives a real browser — opens pages, types into boxes, clicks buttons, reads text — the same way a human would, but at machine speed and without getting bored. That forty-five-minute task became a ninety-second scheduled script. Browser automation is your tool of last resort, and knowing both *how* to use it and *when not to* is the mark of a competent engineer. ##### When to use browser automation — and when not to The hierarchy is strict, and it is what today's assignment asks you to articulate: 1. **Official API** — always first. Structured, stable, documented, fast, permitted. 2. **Data export / webhook / integration** — if the app offers CSV export or a native connector, use it. 3. **Web scraping with `requests`** — if the data is in the HTML of a public page with no login and no JavaScript rendering (tomorrow's topic). 4. **Browser automation** — when the task requires logging in, clicking through multi-step flows, interacting with JavaScript-heavy interfaces, or submitting forms. Reasons you legitimately end up at step 4: no API exists; the API exists but lacks the specific operation you need; the site is a single-page app that renders everything with JavaScript so the raw HTML is empty; the workflow requires authentication with session cookies; or you must *submit* data, not just read it. Reasons you should **not** be at step 4: an API exists and you did not check; the site's terms of service prohibit it; you are hammering someone's server; or you are automating something involving other people's personal data without a legal basis. ##### Selenium versus Playwright **Selenium** (2004) is the veteran. Enormous community, works with every browser and every language, and it is what most enterprise QA teams already run. Its age shows: the API is more verbose, and it historically required manual driver management and explicit waits everywhere. **Playwright** (Microsoft, 2020) learned from Selenium's two decades of pain. It bundles its own browsers, supports Chromium, Firefox and WebKit from one API, and — crucially — has **auto-waiting** built into every action. Before clicking, Playwright automatically waits for the element to exist, be visible, be stable, be enabled, and receive events. That single design decision eliminates the majority of flaky-test bugs that plague Selenium scripts. For new automation work in 2026, **Playwright is the better default**. Learn Selenium when you join a team that already uses it. ```bash pip install playwright playwright install chromium # downloads the browser binary ``` ##### Locating elements: selectors Your script needs to tell the browser *which* element to interact with. This is the skill that determines whether your automation is robust or fragile. Open the page, right-click the element, choose **Inspect**, and look at the HTML. Then choose a locator, in this order of preference: | Strategy | Example | Robustness | |---|---|---| | **Test ID** | `page.get_by_test_id("submit-btn")` | Best — added specifically for automation | | **Role + name** | `page.get_by_role("button", name="Search")` | Excellent — semantic, matches how users see it | | **Label** | `page.get_by_label("Email address")` | Excellent for form fields | | **Text** | `page.get_by_text("Sign in")` | Good, but breaks on wording/language changes | | **CSS selector** | `page.locator("#search-input")` | Fine if the ID is stable | | **XPath** | `page.locator("//div[3]/span[2]")` | Worst — position-based, breaks constantly | The principle: **locate elements the way a human identifies them** — by their visible label, role or text — not by their position in the DOM tree. A selector like `div > div > div:nth-child(4) > span` is a promise to break the next time a designer adds a wrapper div. CSS selector basics you should know: `#id`, `.class`, `tag`, `[attribute="value"]`, `parent > child` (direct child), `ancestor descendant` (any depth). ##### Clicking, typing, and navigating Here is the practical task, written as a complete Playwright script: ```python from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright def search_quotes(term: str, max_results: int = 5) -> list[str]: """Open a demo site, search, and return the first few result texts.""" with sync_playwright() as p: browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True) context = browser.new_context( viewport={"width": 1280, "height": 800}, user_agent="Mozilla/5.0 (automation practice script)", ) page = context.new_page() try: page.goto("https://quotes.toscrape.com/search.aspx", wait_until="domcontentloaded", timeout=30_000) # Interact: choose an author, then a tag, then submit page.select_option("#author", label="Albert Einstein") page.wait_for_timeout(500) # let the dependent dropdown refresh page.select_option("#tag", index=1) page.get_by_role("button", name="Search").click() # Wait for results rather than guessing page.wait_for_selector(".quote", timeout=15_000) quotes = page.locator(".quote .content").all_inner_texts() page.screenshot(path="results.png", full_page=True) return quotes[:max_results] except Exception as e: page.screenshot(path="error.png") # invaluable for debugging print(f"Automation failed: {e}") return [] finally: context.close() browser.close() if __name__ == "__main__": for i, q in enumerate(search_quotes("einstein"), start=1): print(f"{i}. {q[:80]}") ``` The core action vocabulary: ```python page.goto(url) # navigate page.fill("#email", "ananya@example.com") # clear and type page.type("#search", "keyboard", delay=50) # keystroke-by-keystroke page.click("text=Submit") # click page.check("#terms") # checkbox page.select_option("#country", "IN") # dropdown page.set_input_files("#upload", "doc.pdf") # file upload page.press("#search", "Enter") # keyboard key page.go_back() # history page.inner_text(".title") # read text page.get_attribute("a.link", "href") # read an attribute page.locator(".item").count() # count matches page.screenshot(path="page.png") # capture ``` ##### Waiting: the difference between reliable and flaky This is the single most important reliability concept, and the assignment asks you to explain it. Web pages are asynchronous. When you click "Search," the browser sends a request, waits, receives data, and renders results — over hundreds or thousands of milliseconds. If your script tries to read the results the instant after clicking, they do not exist yet, and you get an error. On a fast connection it might work; on a slow one it fails. That intermittent, environment-dependent failure is called **flakiness**, and it is the plague of browser automation (systematic reviews of web testing, such as Doğan et al. 2014, identify synchronization as the dominant source of unreliable tests). Three kinds of waiting, in order of quality: **Auto-waiting (best).** Playwright does this for you. `page.click("#submit")` internally waits for the element to be attached, visible, stable and enabled before clicking. Most of the time you write no wait code at all. **Explicit conditional waits (good).** Wait for a specific observable condition: ```python page.wait_for_selector(".results-loaded", state="visible", timeout=15_000) page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle") page.wait_for_url("**/dashboard") page.wait_for_function("document.querySelectorAll('.row').length > 10") ``` **Fixed sleeps (worst).** `time.sleep(5)` is either too short (still flaky) or too long (wastes time on every run). Use it only as a last resort for animations or throttling, as in the 500 ms pause above where a dependent dropdown repopulates. ##### Headless mode `headless=True` runs the browser with no visible window — faster, lighter, and required on servers with no display. `headless=False` shows the browser, which is essential while developing because you can *watch* what your script does. Playwright also offers `slow_mo=500` to slow every action down so you can follow along, and a superb `page.pause()` that opens an interactive inspector. Two production notes: some sites detect headless browsers and behave differently, and running headless on a server means you cannot see failures — so **always screenshot on error**, as the script above does. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Launch browser
headless in prod] --> B[New context
viewport, user agent, cookies] B --> C[goto URL] C --> D[Wait for the page
to be ready] D --> E[Locate elements
by role / label / test-id] E --> F[Interact: fill, click, select] F --> G[Wait for the result
condition, not a sleep] G --> H{Success?} H -->|yes| I[Extract data,
screenshot, save] H -->|no| J[Screenshot + log,
retry or alert] I --> K[Close context & browser] J --> K ``` ##### Why browser automation is fragile Two reasons the assignment asks for, and both are worth stating plainly. **1. It depends on the UI, which changes without notice.** An API is a contract with versioning and deprecation notices. A web page's HTML is an implementation detail the owner can restructure any Tuesday. A renamed CSS class, an added wrapper element, a redesigned login flow — any of these silently breaks your script, and you find out only when it fails. **2. It depends on timing, rendering and environment.** Network latency, JavaScript execution, animations, lazy loading, A/B tests showing different layouts to different sessions, cookie banners appearing intermittently, CAPTCHAs, two-factor prompts, session expiry. An API call has one failure mode; a browser session has dozens. Add to that: it is 10–100× slower than an API call, it consumes far more memory and CPU, and it usually requires storing login credentials. ##### Common pitfalls - **Brittle XPath/position selectors** instead of role, label or test-id. - **`time.sleep()` everywhere** instead of conditional waits. - **No error screenshot** — debugging a headless failure blind is miserable. - **Not closing the browser** — leaked processes eat server memory. - **Ignoring cookie banners and modals** that block your target element. - **Hard-coded credentials** — use environment variables, as always. - **No rate limiting** — a fast loop against someone's site is abusive and will get you blocked. - **Ignoring terms of service** — automating a site that forbids it is a legal and professional risk. - **Not handling the "no results" case** — your script should distinguish "empty" from "broken." ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: install **Playwright** (or Selenium) and write a script that opens a website, fills a search box, submits it, **waits for results**, and extracts the first few result titles. Run it first with `headless=False` and `slow_mo=500` so you can watch it work — genuinely one of the more satisfying moments in this course — then switch to headless. The mini project takes it end to end: log into a demo site (`the-internet.herokuapp.com` and `saucedemo.com` exist precisely for this), navigate to a page, enter data, submit, capture a confirmation, and save the result — **with proper waits so it runs reliably**. Prove the reliability: run it five times in a row and confirm five clean runs. If one fails, you have a waiting bug, and finding it is the real lesson. For the assignment, explain **when browser automation beats an API** (no API exists, missing operation, login-gated, JS-rendered, submission required), give **two reasons it is more fragile** (UI changes without contract or notice; timing/environment variability), and describe **how waiting prevents flakiness** — auto-waiting first, explicit conditional waits second, fixed sleeps only as a last resort. ##### Key takeaways - Browser automation drives a real browser to do what a human would; it is the tool of last resort after APIs, exports and simple scraping. - Playwright is the better modern default thanks to bundled browsers, cross-engine support and built-in auto-waiting; Selenium remains common in existing teams. - Locate elements the way humans identify them — test ID, role, label, text — never by DOM position. - Waiting is the reliability skill: rely on auto-waiting, use explicit conditional waits when needed, and avoid fixed sleeps. - Expect fragility: UIs change without notice and timing varies, so screenshot on error, close browsers properly, respect terms of service, and rate-limit yourself.
